subject: math
domain: Statistics and Probability — Making Inferences and Justifying Conclusions
cluster: Make inferences and justify conclusions from sample surveys, experiments, and observational studies
description: Students use data from a single random sample to produce a point estimate of an unknown population parameter and then attach a margin of error to that estimate. For a quantitative variable they take the sample mean $\bar{x}$ as the estimate of the population mean $\mu$; for a categorical variable they take the sample proportion $\hat{p}=\dfrac{x}{n}$ as the estimate of the population proportion $p$. They build a margin of error two ways: first conceptually, by reading the spread of an empirical sampling distribution generated by a simulation (many resamples of size $n$), and second by formula, computing the standard error and a margin of error $\text{ME}$ for $95\%$ confidence using $\text{ME}\approx 2\cdot SE$, where $SE_{\hat{p}}=\sqrt{\dfrac{\hat{p}(1-\hat{p})}{n}}$ for a proportion and $SE_{\bar{x}}=\dfrac{s}{\sqrt{n}}$ for a mean. They report the result as an interval estimate $\text{(estimate)}\pm\text{ME}$, interpret what that interval and confidence level mean, and reason about how the margin of error shrinks as the sample size $n$ grows (roughly as $\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{n}}$).
subSkills: Compute a point estimate of a population mean from a sample with $\bar{x}=\dfrac{\sum x_i}{n}$
Compute a point estimate of a population proportion with $\hat{p}=\dfrac{x}{n}$
Read the center and spread of an empirical sampling distribution produced by a simulation of repeated random samples
Estimate a margin of error from a simulation as the half-width of the middle $95\%$ of the simulated estimates (about $2$ standard deviations of the simulated distribution)
Compute the standard error of a proportion, $SE_{\hat{p}}=\sqrt{\dfrac{\hat{p}(1-\hat{p})}{n}}$
Compute the standard error of a mean, $SE_{\bar{x}}=\dfrac{s}{\sqrt{n}}$
Compute a $95\%$ margin of error with $\text{ME}\approx 2\cdot SE$ and build the interval $\text{estimate}\pm\text{ME}$
Interpret a confidence interval and the meaning of a margin of error in the context of the survey
Reason about how the margin of error changes (shrinks like $\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{n}}$) as the sample size increases
Distinguish a parameter (fixed population value) from a statistic (varies sample to sample) and identify why simulation is needed

problemArchetypes.name: Point estimate of a proportion
problemArchetypes.example: In a random sample of $200$ voters, $116$ support a measure. Estimate the population proportion: $\hat{p}=\dfrac{116}{200}=0.58$.

problemArchetypes.name: Point estimate of a mean
problemArchetypes.example: A random sample of $5$ commute times (minutes) is $22,18,25,30,20$. Estimate the population mean commute: $\bar{x}=\dfrac{22+18+25+30+20}{5}=\dfrac{115}{5}=23$ minutes.

problemArchetypes.name: Read a margin of error off a simulation
problemArchetypes.example: A simulation resamples $n=50$ and produces sample proportions whose middle $95\%$ run from $0.46$ to $0.62$, centered at $0.54$. The margin of error is half the width: $\dfrac{0.62-0.46}{2}=0.08$, so the estimate is $0.54\pm 0.08$.

problemArchetypes.name: Margin of error for a proportion by formula
Margin of error for a mean by formula
problemArchetypes.example: A sample of $n=64$ has $\bar{x}=23$ and $s=8$. Then $SE=\dfrac{8}{\sqrt{64}}=\dfrac{8}{8}=1$, so $\text{ME}\approx 2(1)=2$ and the interval is $23\pm 2$ minutes.

problemArchetypes.name: Build and interpret the interval
problemArchetypes.example: From $\hat{p}=0.58$ and $\text{ME}=0.07$, the $95\%$ interval is $0.58\pm 0.07$, i.e. $0.51$ to $0.65$. We are $95\%$ confident the true proportion of all voters who support the measure lies between $51\%$ and $65\%$.

problemArchetypes.name: Effect of sample size on margin of error
problemArchetypes.example: A poll with $n=400$ has margin of error $0.05$. To cut the margin of error in half to $0.025$, the sample size must grow by a factor of $4$ (since $\text{ME}\propto\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{n}}$), to $n=1600$.

problemArchetypes.name: Parameter vs. statistic / why simulate
problemArchetypes.example: Identify which value is the parameter and which is the statistic: the true mean weight $\mu$ of all boxes is the parameter; the sample mean $\bar{x}=24.7$ from $30$ boxes is the statistic, and resampling shows how much $\bar{x}$ would vary, which is what the margin of error measures.

Easy.description: Single-step computation of a point estimate, or reading a margin of error and interval directly off a fully described simulation, or distinguishing parameter from statistic. tier1 lives here and ramps into Medium.
constraints: Proportion items give the count $x$ and sample size $n$ and ask only for $\hat{p}=\dfrac{x}{n}$, with $n$ a round number ($n=100,200,$ etc.) so the division is clean
Mean items give a short list of $4$ to $6$ whole-number values and ask only for $\bar{x}$
Simulation items state the center and the endpoints of the middle $95\%$; the task is the single subtraction-and-halving for $\text{ME}$, or naming the resulting interval
Vocabulary items ask the student to label a stated value as the parameter or the statistic with no computation

Medium.description: Compute a standard error and a $95\%$ margin of error by formula, then assemble and state the interval, or interpret a confidence interval in context. tier1 ends here and tier2 begins here.
constraints: Proportion items require $SE=\sqrt{\dfrac{\hat{p}(1-\hat{p})}{n}}$ then $\text{ME}\approx 2\cdot SE$, with $\hat{p}$ already given or a one-step computation away
Mean items give $\bar{x}$, the sample standard deviation $s$, and a perfect-square $n$ ($n=16,25,36,64,100$) so $\sqrt{n}$ and $SE=\dfrac{s}{\sqrt{n}}$ are exact
Student must combine the point estimate with the margin of error to state $\text{estimate}\pm\text{ME}$ and the endpoint interval
Interpretation items ask for a one-sentence reading of a $95\%$ confidence interval in the survey's context

Hard.description: Multi-step reasoning that chains estimate, standard error, and interpretation, or works backward, or reasons about the $\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{n}}$ relationship between sample size and margin of error. tier2 lives here.
constraints: Reason about sample size: given a target margin of error, find the $n$ needed, using $\text{ME}\propto\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{n}}$ (quadrupling $n$ halves $\text{ME}$)
Work backward: recover $n$, $x$, or $\hat{p}$ from a stated margin of error or interval
Chain the full pipeline: from raw counts or a data list, compute the estimate, the standard error, the margin of error, the interval, and a contextual interpretation
Compare two studies or two sample sizes and justify in a sentence which gives the more precise estimate and why
Judge a claim about a confidence interval or margin of error and explain the flaw (e.g. confusing the interval with a probability about one fixed parameter)

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Student treats the margin of error as the standard error itself, dropping the factor of about $2$ for $95\%$ confidence
Student omits the reciprocal sample size and uses $\sqrt{\hat{p}(1-\hat{p})}$ without dividing by $n$
Student uses $n$ instead of $\sqrt{n}$ in the standard error of a mean
Student reads the full width of the middle $95\%$ of a simulation as the margin of error instead of the half-width
commonMisconceptions.distractor: For a simulated range $0.46$ to $0.62$ reports $\text{ME}=0.62-0.46=0.16$ instead of $\dfrac{0.62-0.46}{2}=0.08$

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Student believes the margin of error shrinks in direct proportion to $n$ rather than to $\sqrt{n}$
commonMisconceptions.distractor: Claims doubling the sample size from $400$ to $800$ halves the margin of error, instead of recognizing that halving $\text{ME}$ requires quadrupling $n$ to $1600$

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Student uses the population size instead of the sample size in the standard error, assuming a bigger population means a bigger margin of error
commonMisconceptions.distractor: Uses the city's $50000$ residents in place of $n=200$ in the denominator, instead of recognizing the margin of error depends on the sample size, not the population size

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Student interprets a $95\%$ confidence interval as a probability statement about the sample statistic rather than a bound on the population parameter
commonMisconceptions.distractor: Says there is a $95\%$ chance the sample proportion $\hat{p}=0.58$ falls in the interval, instead of being $95\%$ confident the true population proportion $p$ lies in $0.51$ to $0.65$

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Student adds the margin of error to one side only or applies it to the count rather than the proportion
commonMisconceptions.distractor: Reports the interval as $0.58$ to $0.65$ (one-sided) instead of $0.58\pm 0.07$, i.e. $0.51$ to $0.65$
